candidates.title: The Truth Beneath
candidates.reason: Over its 102-103-minute narrative, a politician's daughter disappears during an election campaign, and her mother Yeon-hong uncovers evidence in successive stages: the girl's supposed destination was a false lead; a bullied classmate has her expensive watch; leaked exam papers and an apparent teacher's secret complicate the search; a body is found; a lie-detector result and the classmate's connection to the family driver challenge the first murder theory; and a hidden cache of money leads to a recorded affair, blackmail, and the actual circumstances of the killing. The final confrontation exposes the husband's involvement in hiring a killer without realizing his daughter was a target. These are distinct answers in the early, middle and final sections, not just an investigation that withholds all information until the end, although the largest culpability reversal remains late. Screen Daily praises the accomplished fragmented editing, visual design and central performance; The Hollywood News specifically notes that new answers arrive repeatedly and shift the viewer's theories. AsianMovieWeb agrees that surprises recur but criticizes an initially slow political setup, occasional implausible coincidences and an occasionally unfocused mixture of grief, school bullying and political satire. Korea JoongAng Daily likewise identifies tonal inconsistency despite sustained tension. The film is a visually polished maternal investigation and psychological mystery, with real emotional drama and limited physical action; the political setting should not be inflated into a sprawling institutional conspiracy.

candidates.title: The Interview
candidates.reason: The Australian 103-104-minute psychological thriller confines most of its action to a police interrogation. The initial arrest seems to concern a stolen car, but detectives connect its owner to missing-person cases and a suspected serial killer. The apparently helpless Eddie Fleming grows assertive, delivers a detailed confession, then withdraws it on the grounds of coercion. A separate revelation that internal affairs secretly recorded the questioning destroys the evidentiary value of the confession, while Steele's counter-recording of an ethics investigator further reverses the power dynamic. Fleming's final departure leaves his actual guilt unresolved. The car-theft lead, missing-person implications, confession, recantation and covert-monitoring disclosures provide several meaningful stages of reframing, though the long exchanges between them are not themselves frequent new answers. SBS praises the multi-layered screenplay, performances and controlled cinematography; The Guardian emphasizes the suspect-versus-detective duel and a major mid-film turn. A contrary review at The Ace Black Movie Blog finds the questioning linear, the reporter subplot distracting and the momentum uneven. This is an intense, talk-heavy psychological and evidence-integrity mystery with almost no physical action. Its grey-green, older-era visual language is distinct from its accomplished photographic craft, and its ending preserves ambiguity rather than resolving a conventional culprit hunt.
